summary: This informational memo introduces TESLA, a method that lets every receiver of a multicast or broadcast stream check the integrity and source of each packet. It needs no trust between receivers and uses little work per packet.

eli5.summary: When one sender talks to many listeners, each should be sure the words really came from the sender. TESLA gives each packet a proof that is cheap to check.

questions: how does tesla authenticate multicast packets
what is key disclosure delay in tesla
why cant mac be used for multicast
subtitle: How one sender can prove to millions of receivers that each packet is genuine, using symmetric keys that are revealed on a schedule.

tldr.problem: A multicast or broadcast sender cannot use a shared MAC key, because every receiver would know it and could forge packets. Digital signatures on every packet are too costly.
tldr.mechanism: TESLA attaches a MAC to each packet, keyed with a key from a one-way chain that the sender only reveals a few time intervals later. Receivers with loosely synchronized clocks buffer packets and check them when the key arrives.
tldr.outcome: Receivers get cheap, loss-tolerant per-packet source authentication with a short delay, but no non-repudiation. This memo is informational and is meant to help write standardizable TESLA-based protocols.

facts.label: Minimum workable delay
facts.value: d of 2 or more; d=1 does not work

facts.label: Symmetric vs asymmetric
facts.value: 3 to 5 orders of magnitude more efficient

today: RFC 4082 is an Informational RFC from June 2005, and no other RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It states that it is intended to assist in writing standardizable and secure specifications for protocols based on TESLA in different contexts.

sections.title: Why Multicast Needs a New Approach
sections.content:
In multicast, one packet can reach millions of receivers, and so can a malicious one. Source authentication lets receivers confirm that a packet came from the right source.

In unicast, sender and receiver share a secret key and compute a message authentication code (MAC) over the data. That is not secure for broadcast: every receiver knows the MAC key, so any of them could impersonate the sender to the others. What is needed is asymmetry: anyone can verify, but only the sender can produce.

Digital signatures have that property, but they cost a lot of computation and usually bandwidth. Because the sender does not retransmit lost packets and receivers want to check each packet immediately, a signature would be needed on every packet. The RFC notes that symmetric cryptography is in general 3 to 5 orders of magnitude more efficient than asymmetric cryptography.
sections.eli5: If everyone in a class knows the same secret handshake, anyone could pretend to be the teacher. Signing every note with a fancy stamp works but is slow, so TESLA finds a cheaper trick.

sections.title: Delayed Key Disclosure
sections.content:
TESLA uses mainly symmetric cryptography and gets its asymmetry from time. Sender and receivers are loosely time-synchronized. The sender builds a one-way chain of keys and ties each key to a time interval.

  • The sender puts a MAC on each packet, using the key for the current interval.
  • It discloses that key later. For example, the key used in interval i is disclosed in interval i+3.
  • A receiver checks that the key was not yet disclosed when the packet was sent. If so it buffers the packet. Otherwise the packet is dropped because it cannot be authenticated.
  • When the key arrives, the receiver checks that it belongs to the chain and then checks the MAC.

Because earlier chain values can be recomputed from later ones, a receiver can still check earlier packets even when some key disclosures are lost. The delay in practice is on the order of one round-trip time.

TESLA does not support non-repudiation. A receiver can know a stream is authentic but cannot prove that to a third party.
sections.eli5: The teacher locks each note and shares the key a bit later. By then the notes are already delivered, so nobody can swap one using the key, and everyone can check them once the key shows up.

sections.title: Sender Setup and Receiver Bootstrap
sections.content:
The sender divides time into intervals of length T_int and picks a chain length N, which limits how long it can transmit before building a new chain. It picks a random K_N and computes the rest recursively with K_i = F(K_{i+1}), where F(k) = f_k(0) and f is a pseudo-random function. Key K_i serves packets sent in interval i. A second function F' derives the actual MAC key K'_i = F'(K_i), so the same key is not used for two cryptographic purposes.

A receiver needs three things before it can authenticate: an upper bound D_t on how far its clock lags the sender's, one authenticated key of the chain (typically K_0, signed by the sender), and the disclosure schedule (T_int, T_0, N and the delay d). TESLA MUST be bootstrapped through a regular data authentication system, for example a digital signature.

For direct time synchronization the receiver sends a sync message, the sender replies with its own time, and the receiver sets D_t = t_s - t_r + S, where S bounds clock drift. The exchange itself needs to be authenticated. The security of TESLA does not depend on any assumption about network delay.
sections.eli5: Before the show starts, each listener gets a signed starting clue and agrees roughly what time it is. After that they only have to listen.

sections.title: Sending and Checking Packets
sections.content:
To send message M_j in interval i, the sender builds the packet P_j = {M_j || i || MAC(K'_i, M_j) || K_{i-d}}. Each packet therefore carries the key from d intervals ago, and d is the key disclosure delay.

The receiver runs these steps in order:

  1. Safe packet test: record the arrival time, compute an upper bound on the sender's clock, and verify the sender is not yet in the interval where it discloses K_i. Safe packets are buffered; unsafe ones should be discarded.
  2. New key index test: check whether a key with the same or a later index has already been disclosed.
  3. Key verification test: check that the new key hashes back to an earlier disclosed key. If not, discard the packet.
  4. Message verification: recompute the MAC for buffered packets of that interval and release those that match.

For choosing d, the RFC recommends d = ceil(2m / T_int) + 1 when 2m is a reasonable upper bound on round-trip time. A disclosure delay of one interval (d=1) does not work. A d that is too short makes packets unverifiable; one that is too long delays authentication.
sections.eli5: Each note carries an old key from a few turns ago. The listener first checks the note arrived before its key could have been shared, keeps it, and unlocks it once the key arrives.

sections.title: Denial of Service and Security Notes
sections.content:
Because receivers buffer packets before they can verify them, a flood of bogus packets could fill their buffers. Any receiver can add simple checks without protocol changes: a session validity test (source address and port, no replays, no unusually large packets) and a reasonable misordering test that bounds how far along the hash chain a receiver will look. The bound g starts at g_max (say, 16) and drops to g_min (typically 1) after a failure.

Stronger protection needs extra measures on both ends. The RFC outlines three: adding a group MAC to each packet, never re-using a MAC key so that each packet reveals a new key, and moving buffering to the sender. The first needs a larger per-packet overhead; the second needs two hashes per packet and a longer chain.

The Security Considerations section calls verification of the timing conditions by far the most delicate point. A change to the key disclosure schedule should never be announced inside the stream itself. If the verifier is separate from the application, a trusted channel must exist between them.
sections.eli5: A prankster could stuff a listener's mailbox with fake notes. So listeners check each note's envelope quickly and ignore ones that look odd.

sections.title: Where to Place TESLA
sections.content:
TESLA can run at the network, transport or application layer. In the network layer, upper layers see only authenticated data, which helps against denial of service. In the transport or application layer the network layer stays unchanged, but buffering in the transport may add unpredictable delay.

TESLA relies on packet timing, so running it on a layer that aggressively buffers packets and hides true arrival times will significantly reduce performance. Two extensions are mentioned: several chains per stream with different disclosure delays, and sender-side buffering. To authenticate the last part of a message, the sender must send an empty message carrying the key.
sections.eli5: It matters where in the postal chain you check the notes. Check early and everyone downstream gets only good notes, but check late and you do not have to change the post office.

data.title: TESLA packet and keys
data.code:
K_i  = F(K_{i+1})        one-way key chain
K'_i = F'(K_i)           MAC key for interval i
P_j  = {M_j || i || MAC(K'_i, M_j) || K_{i-d}}
d    = ceil(2m / T_int) + 1

items.title: Low overhead
items.text: Low computation and communication cost to generate and verify.

items.title: Loss tolerant
items.text: Tolerates any level of loss without retransmissions.

items.title: Scalable
items.text: No per-receiver state at the sender.

items.title: Timing needed
items.text: Receivers must be loosely time-synchronized with the source.

items.title: No non-repudiation
items.text: Receivers cannot prove authenticity to third parties.
